title: Oil Crashes 15 Per Cent as Trump Floats Iran Ceasefire — Indian Markets and NRI Portfolios Stand to Gain Big
excerpt: Crude plunges to $95 a barrel and stock futures surge worldwide after Washington signals a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, potentially slashing India’s import bill by billions
body:
Global oil prices plunged 15 per cent on Sunday after reports emerged that the Trump administration is floating a ceasefire deal in the Iran conflict, sending US crude tumbling to $95 a barrel from recent highs above $110 and sparking a broad rally across stock futures worldwide. GIFT Nifty, the offshore indicator for India’s benchmark index, jumped sharply in early trading, signalling that Monday’s session on Dalal Street could open with significant gains.

The proposed deal, which remains preliminary, would require Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint through which roughly 20 per cent of the world’s oil supply passes — in exchange for a pause in military operations. Israel has reportedly agreed to a two-week operational pause as a confidence-building measure. The arrangement falls short of a comprehensive peace agreement, and analysts warn that the deal could unravel quickly given the depth of hostilities, but markets are treating even a temporary reprieve as a major positive catalyst.

The S&P 500 futures gained 0.4 per cent and the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.7 per cent in overnight trading, while Brent crude fell to $97 from $112, its steepest single-session drop since the onset of the conflict. European futures also pointed higher, with energy-importing economies across Asia expected to be among the biggest beneficiaries.

India imports approximately 85 per cent of its crude oil, making it the world’s third-largest oil consumer and one of the economies most sensitive to price swings. Every $10 drop in crude prices saves India an estimated $15 to $17 billion annually on its import bill, eases pressure on the current account deficit, and gives the Reserve Bank of India more room to hold or cut interest rates.

The timing is particularly significant. India’s wholesale price inflation surged to a 42-month high of 8.3 per cent in recent data, driven almost entirely by fuel and commodity costs. A sustained decline in crude prices would take pressure off both wholesale and consumer inflation, potentially allowing the RBI to resume its easing cycle — a development that would be bullish for both equity and bond markets.

Non-Resident Indians with exposure to Indian equities — whether through direct stock holdings, mutual fund SIPs, or India-focused ETFs — are positioned for a meaningful uplift if the ceasefire holds. Sectors likely to benefit most include airlines and logistics, where jet fuel is the single largest cost for carriers like IndiGo and Air India; paints and chemicals companies like Asian Paints and Pidilite that use petroleum derivatives as raw materials; autos and consumer goods, where lower fuel costs boost spending power particularly in rural India; and banks, where an RBI rate cut would boost net interest margins and loan growth.

Conversely, upstream oil producers like ONGC and Oil India could face headwinds from lower realisations, though this is typically offset by reduced government subsidy burdens.

Markets have been burned before by premature optimism on Iran. The Strait of Hormuz has been a geopolitical weapon for decades, and Iran’s willingness to genuinely demilitarise the waterway remains unproven. Traders are pricing in a probability, not a certainty, and crude could snap back violently if talks collapse.

For NRI investors, the prudent approach is to stay invested rather than chase the rally, and to avoid making large tactical bets on a single geopolitical outcome. The structural case for Indian equities — driven by demographics, digitisation, and manufacturing shift — remains intact regardless of whether oil is at $95 or $110. The ceasefire, if it holds, simply makes that case cheaper to access.
